posts.name: Kris Sidial🇺🇸
posts.text:
Everyone who keeps sharing these short interest charts is missing the flows behind them. Most shops are not taking outright short bets. This is another effort to ease margin requirements across the street: banks providing balance sheet for more speculative bets are asking clients to post more short exposure.

The sequence on the street looks like this:

HF manager: “I want more margin.”

Bank: “Things look risky in public AI bets, and we’re already lending a lot against private AI bets. For some clients, we’ll extend more financing, but only if they add more short exposure to improve their collateral scores.”

HF manager: “Okay, I’ll short more stock against my main bet.”

That is how you end up with short exposures that look astronomically high while many end users remain heavily long tech. The additional shorts are supporting the financing of their main bets.

Which also tells the bigger story on why raw equity financing rates haven’t blown out the way they did ahead of the big SpaceX IPO in June, despite the fact that lending is slowing.

posts.text:
In early 2002, Elon was preparing to launch SpaceX and searching for the people who could help him build a rocket from scratch. One Sunday in January 2002, he walked into a friend's rented warehouse in Huntington Beach and found Tom Mueller holding an 80-pound rocket engine on his shoulder, trying to bolt it to a frame. It was the largest liquid-fuel engine any amateur had ever built, with 13,000 pounds of thrust, made in Tom's spare time. 

Elon asked the main question  “Could you build something bigger?”

The next Sunday Elon came to his house. It was Super Bowl Sunday; they watched maybe one play, because they were too busy sketching the first SpaceX rocket.

Tom became SpaceX employee #1, and the man who built engines on weekends went on to build Merlin, Kestrel and Draco. 

Elon saw a person, not a résumé, someone who built rockets with his own hands simply because he loved them.

The French bond spread, now at 1.69 percentage points, is rapidly approaching the peak reached at the height of the Eurozone debt crisis.

So, are we in a crisis? Will France default?

The answer to the second question is no, assuming the ECB prints money and cuts interest rates when things get really ugly.

Are we in a crisis? Well, that depends.

Not the kind of turmoil we witnessed during the Eurozone debt crisis, when it was unclear whether Greece and Italy could remain in the eurozone.

Many years and countless ECB bond-buying programs later, we know governments and central banks will work together to keep things from falling apart.

Yet I would call this a bond crisis.

Because after nearly six years of negative nominal returns (and an even worse picture after inflation), we now have another painful reminder that bonds are no longer the asset class they once were.

Not only have bonds delivered negative returns, but their risk profile has also deteriorated significantly, while their diversification benefits have largely evaporated.

Bond returns have become positively correlated with equity returns. And I expect that relationship to persist for one simple reason: bonds themselves have become a risky asset.

To be clear, at current yields, bonds could certainly deliver positive returns once interest rates decline.

But that doesn't mean bonds will magically return to being a low-risk asset class offering decent positive returns and meaningful diversification.

posts.name: Byrne Hobart
posts.text:
This is not a very good point, and it doesn't advance the discussion at all. There is an enormous burden of proof on you to argue that giving additional dollars to California is net beneficial, whereas the equity and bond markets' willingness to finance an expensive AI buildout provides ample evidence that people who know what they're talking about believe that dollars in the hands of these tech executives will produce something of value. Maybe you're smarter than all of them, but the way you advocate this wealth tax implies that you're going to great lengths to disguise this.

Further, your point about the cyclicality of this tax revenue accidentally raises another point that is very damaging to your campaign. California's tax system is already cyclical! They're already overreliant on a small number of taxpayers compared to other states (different ones each year, but for CA to work it really needs to be the place where successful tech executives want to realize liquidity). The top 1% paid half the state's income taxes in 2021—then 40% less a year later, because tech stocks went down.

A one-time wealth tax theoretically avoids this, because you just levy it when assets are expensive. But as far as I can tell, the plan is to spend the money in five years and hope somebody else has solve the state's budget problems by then. This is not what people conventionally refer to as a "plan." So I take Zucman at his word (iffy proposition!) when he says he wants it to be a regular thing. 

If we're going to tax a form of wealth, I have an idea should really tickle you as an economist, or at least as a guy who probably hangs out with them from time to time: tax the land! It's a broader tax base, land values are far more stable than equity, and land, of course, cannot hop on its private jet and head to Miami. This also has a salutary effect on California politics, by sending every homeowner in the state a shocking bill from time to time. This will get voters asking themselves the same question you refuse to answer: what good is the state doing with all of that money?

I still find it puzzling that you're making such unsophisticated arguments, here. Surely, you can do better, and can explain what it is that the government California will do with another few billion dollars that it hasn't accomplished with the first $350bn or so.

As I've shown you a few times now, it's entirely possible to have a well-informed, reasonable argument about the proposed wealth tax. All you have to do is switch sides.

posts.text:
A new coalition, the Association for Direct Care, has launched with a mix of health systems, physician advocacy, and employer-purchaser muscle behind it.

The mission is to get more employers and clinicians dealing directly with each other, cut out the administrative bloat, and bring some transparency to how care gets purchased.

Alyssa Simpson Rochwerger, co-founder and CEO of Grounded Health @getgroundedhlth, which joined the coalition, explained, “Every other dollar a company spends is visible. Finance can see software spend, travel spend, payroll — down to the transaction. Healthcare is the one place where an employer pays the bill and never sees the receipt.”

Direct contracting is being pitched as the fix: real access to claims and pricing data, less middleman, more accountability.

What they're actually asking for:

• Expanding direct contracting across commercial markets and federal health programs
• Better access to healthcare data
• Fewer regulatory/administrative barriers standing between patients, employers, and providers

I have to wonder how much traction this gets with Congress in the near term, but the timing tracks. Indiana's already built laws specifically enabling direct-to-employer arrangements, and groups like this tend to be a signal that a policy push is coming, not just a press release. 

Worth keeping an eye on who else joins in the coming months.

Press release: https://employerdirectcare.org/association-for-direct-care-launches-to-lower-health-care-costs-and-expand-direct-contracting/
Learn more: https://employerdirectcare.org/
